# The Department of Unclaimed Things

On the morning the city abolished its lost-property office, a man came in to claim a ladder.

“How long ago did you lose it?” Mara asked.

“Forty-three years.”

She looked up. He had the mild, expectant face of someone who had just asked for a glass of water.

“Do you remember where?”

“Outside my house. Or it was my house then. I put the ladder up to paint the bedroom window, and my wife said the baby had finally gone to sleep, so I came inside to see. I meant to go back out.”

“And when you did?”

“We had supper. Then it rained for three days. By Sunday the ladder was gone.”

Mara explained that the city generally kept things for ninety days, with exceptions for items of unusual value. She left out the fact that, by noon, the city would no longer keep things at all.

“I thought I might have lent it to someone,” the man said. “I’ve spent forty-three years being a little annoyed with everyone I knew then.”

“Why look for it now?”

“I was annoyed with somebody else this morning and realized I could actually ask him.”

Mara opened the city’s inventory. There were two ladders: an aluminum stepladder recovered from a tram shelter and a wooden ladder retrieved from the canal last November. The man considered both descriptions.

“Mine was wooden.”

“Was it painted?”

“I never got as far as opening the paint.”

She took him down to the basement. The canal ladder had seven rungs, one of them split, and smelled faintly of the canal despite having spent a winter beside a radiator. The man put his hand on it.

“Well,” he said. “That’s not it.”

Mara waited for him to take his hand away. He didn’t.

“You can have it if you want,” she said. “Though I wouldn’t climb it.”

“I wouldn’t climb mine either, at this point.”

They carried it up together. At the door he handed her a claim ticket. She had assumed he didn’t have one. It was a yellow rectangle with a number in the upper corner and a blue ink drawing of a ladder on the back.

“My daughter made that,” he said. “She was six. Not the baby in the story. The next one. She went through a period of giving me receipts for things.”

After he left, Mara turned the ticket over. Under the ladder her predecessor, or her predecessor’s predecessor, had written, *No ladder matching description found. Please try again in thirty days.*

Apparently he had.

At nine, the truck arrived. Two men in orange vests began moving the contents of the basement into the street. A woman from Procurement stood by with a clipboard to determine which objects were suitable for resale. She put a green sticker on a saxophone, a red one on a damp box of wigs, and no sticker at all on a portrait of a boy holding a fish. After some thought she turned the portrait to face the wall.

“Are we taking the shelves?” one of the men asked.

“Those belong to the building.”

“Are we taking the building?”

The woman checked a separate sheet. “Not today.”

Mara went upstairs. Her desk drawers were empty except for a packet of instant soup and the index card she had been carrying from job to job since she was twenty-two. In her brother’s handwriting, the card said: *If they ask about the goat, you were never in Belgium.*

Her brother had written it on the train home from their aunt’s funeral. There had been no goat, and Belgium had been their aunt’s home for twenty years. He’d slipped the card into Mara’s coat pocket while she slept. She found it at customs and began to laugh so hard that the officer moved her out of the queue.

For years she had thought the card would be the thing she would save from a fire. Now that she was actually clearing out a desk, she put it in the bag with the soup and felt mildly cheated. There ought to have been more occasion to it.

The telephone rang.

“Lost property,” Mara said.

“I left a blue jar on the number four bus,” said a woman. “It’s about the size of a large orange.”

“When?”

“Yesterday afternoon. This is extremely important.”

Mara looked through the morning deliveries. Gloves, keys, a transparent bag containing one black shoe and a flyer for a second shoe at half price. At the bottom sat a blue jar with a screw top.

“Can you describe what’s inside?”

“Rice.”

Mara lifted the jar. Something shuffled against the glass.

“Only rice?”

“Yes. How soon can I get there?”

“I don’t know where you’re coming from.”

“Neither do I, exactly. I got off the bus.”

Mara talked the woman to a street sign, then told her how to get to the office. She set the jar aside. A moment later she moved it farther from the edge of the desk.

By ten the street outside looked like the yard of a house whose occupants had separated on unusually generous terms. There were badminton rackets, school uniforms, an electric kettle, a red bicycle with no saddle, and a saddle with no bicycle. A pair of matching suitcases had been lost six months apart, on different bus routes. They had finally met in the basement, where Mara stored one inside the other.

People began to stop. The woman from Procurement explained that nothing could be sold until it had been assessed and listed. A young man asked whether he could have the fish portrait.

“You know him?” she asked.

“No.”

“What do you want it for?”

“My flat is very quiet.”

She looked at him, then at the boy, who had the startled expression of someone beginning to suspect the fish was not going to help. She gave the young man the portrait.

This started something. A delivery cyclist took a pair of ski goggles. A woman in a cream suit tried on a purple wig from the damp box, examined herself in the side mirror of the truck, and asked whether it came in any other colors. One of the men in orange found a tape measure he said was better than his, then pulled his own from his pocket and showed Mara precisely why. The woman from Procurement made a new column on her sheet and labeled it *Other*.

Mara’s brother called at ten thirty.

“Are you a private citizen yet?” he asked.

“I’ve got an hour and a half.”

“Come for lunch. I’ll make you a sandwich that reflects your former rank.”

He lived across the city, in the house he had moved into after his divorce. For the first six months he had owned one plate and seventeen lamps. Mara used to go over on Thursdays to watch television with him. He switched on every lamp as the daylight went, without ever mentioning it. Recently he had acquired a dining table, and at Christmas he’d asked her to bring chairs.

“What rank was that?” she said.

“You tell me how thick to cut the cheese.”

She said she would call him later. Then she took the index card out of her bag and called him back.

“Why Belgium?” she asked.

“What?”

“On the note about the goat.”

There was a pause. She could hear a cupboard opening.

“Because I bought you a goat,” he said. “At the station. A little wooden one. You said you didn’t want anything to remember the trip by, so I was going to hide it in your coat and give you the card as well. Then I dropped the goat between the train and the platform.”

“You never told me that.”

“I thought you’d be upset.”

“I’d have been delighted about the goat.”

“No, I mean I thought you’d be upset that I’d dropped it. You were upset when I ate the last pear.”

She remembered the pear. They had been in their aunt’s kitchen, in the middle of deciding what to do with thirty years of jam jars. He had asked her whether she wanted half and she’d said no. When she heard him bite into it, she had to go out into the garden. There, for want of anything else to do, she righted a fallen flowerpot. It was full of ants, which had presumably preferred it the other way.

“Cut the cheese thick,” she said.

At eleven the woman arrived for the blue jar. She was younger than Mara had imagined and wore a coat with one sleeve turned inside out. She spotted the jar on the desk, put both hands flat on the counter, and exhaled.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“What for?”

“I was going to tell you there were ashes in it, in case you didn’t take the rice seriously. Then I thought if you found it you might open it and be disappointed.”

“Is the rice special?”

“No. I mean it’s not a special kind of rice.” She picked up the jar. “My son’s teacher gave everybody a bean to germinate. We’ve been waiting for it for a week. I moved it from the windowsill on Tuesday, and for two days he’s been asking me if I threw it out. He’s at his dad’s now. I was taking it over to show him.”

“The bean’s in there?”

“In a little envelope. The rice is to keep it dry. I looked it up.”

Mara wondered why the woman had decided the bean needed drying when the whole point had been to get it wet. There was probably an afternoon’s worth of explanation in that coat alone.

“Would you like to use the phone?” she asked.

The woman dialed from memory. A man picked up, and they exchanged a few words in the clipped, overly courteous way Mara recognized from listening to her brother call about a missing school jumper. Then there was a long wait. The woman shook the jar once, quietly, as if whatever was in it might answer first.

“Hi,” she said at last. “Remember how I said I put it somewhere safe?”

She listened.

“No,” she said. “You were right about the bus.”

Mara went outside to give her some privacy. The sack of lost keys was still by the steps. Nobody wanted those. People would pick up keys only on the off chance they recognized their own, and just then there was nobody there to try. Mara crouched and sifted through them. There were keys so new you could still see the price of having them cut written in pencil on the paper tag, and keys rubbed smooth at the shoulders by people who had used them every day. One was attached to a flat stone with a hole in the middle. She couldn’t imagine carrying the stone around in her pocket. She could imagine, very well, finding it on a beach and looking for a use for it.

She had worked in lost property for fourteen years. She was good at persuading people to tell her what was actually missing. They might start with the make of a briefcase, but after a little while they would tell her about the broken clasp, the stain on the lining, the smell of a banana they’d forgotten the previous summer. Their certainty came back as they talked. Sometimes it was a pleasure to break the news that the office had no such thing, because by then they knew exactly where else to look.

Other times a person came in with as little information as possible. A woman had once asked about a teddy bear and then, with evident reluctance, revealed that it was actually a rabbit, that its name was Frank, and that it was hers. Mara had found the rabbit in the drawer labeled *Small Animals*. For reasons nobody at the office could remember, this was also where they put false teeth.

She’d liked the job best on days when everybody got what they came for. There hadn’t been many of those. The closest she could remember was a rainy Tuesday when three nearly identical umbrellas had been returned to their owners. An hour later, one of the owners had come back to say she had the wrong one. The other two were never heard from again. As far as Mara knew, they were satisfied.

At half past eleven, one of the men in orange asked what he should do with an upright piano. There had been some confusion about its status. A previous manager had brought it in for an office Christmas party and never taken it home. For eighteen years the staff had been filing reports on top of it. Nobody knew whether it still belonged to the manager, who lived in Spain, or whether it had become municipal furniture through uninterrupted use.

“Can anybody play?” Mara asked.

The woman from Procurement said that she could, a little. She sat on a box of unclaimed scarves while the two men held the piano steady on the truck’s lift. One note didn’t work and another didn’t stop working when she took her finger off it. She played the tune again, shifting it up, and it went much better. Mara knew it without knowing its name. She waited for the bit she could hum. It turned out to be the end.

“My mother liked that one,” the woman said. She examined her hands, then pulled down the fallboard. “She thought I should do it professionally. She’d never heard a professional.”

At six minutes to twelve the truck left, taking the piano and the keys. The woman from Procurement shook Mara’s hand and asked if she wanted the clipboard.

“Is it yours to give away?”

“It is now,” she said.

Mara went through the ground-floor rooms one last time. The office already smelled different. The objects had brought in their own weather: bus heaters, wet wool, hand cream, the dry heat of handbags left in the sun. Underneath it all was the cool mineral smell of a room whose windows didn’t open.

A girl was waiting at the counter when Mara came back. She was perhaps twelve, with a schoolbag open at the top. Mara nearly told her about the zip, but the girl reached into the bag and took out an envelope instead.

“I found this at the cash machine,” she said.

Inside were two twenty-pound notes and a receipt with the balance still showing. The balance was less than the amount withdrawn. Mara counted the money, though there was very little counting to do.

“Will they come here?” the girl asked.

“Not here. We’re closing.” The girl put a hand out for the envelope, and Mara gave it back. “But the bank’s just down the road. They might be able to work out whose it is.”

“I already tried the bank. The guard said it wasn’t their cash machine.”

“Which machine?”

“The one at the bank.”

Mara looked at the clock. It was twelve. She turned the sign on the door, locked up, and put the keys through the letterbox as instructed. They landed with a sound exactly like keys being put through a letterbox: intimate, ordinary, nothing a person in the street would turn to look at.

“Come on,” she said to the girl. “Show me which guard.”

They walked past the empty patch where the truck had stood. In the window of the café next door, the girl noticed her open schoolbag and stopped to close it. Mara held the envelope while she did. Across the road somebody was carrying a bouquet upside down, shedding water onto the pavement. A bus swung around the corner and Mara took half a step toward it out of habit. She had been catching that bus at the same time, from the same stop, for years. Once, when she’d missed it three mornings in a row, the driver asked on the fourth if she’d been on holiday. She had told him yes. It seemed kinder than telling him about her alarm clock.

The bus pulled away. There would be another one in ten minutes, and one ten minutes after that. The girl tugged on her zip, which had caught in the lining.

“Here,” Mara said. “Hold this a second.”

She handed back the envelope and worked the cloth loose. The trick was to pull the zip a little farther open before trying to close it. When she was done, the girl slid the envelope inside herself. Then she took it out again and carried it in her hand, ready to show the guard.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A carefully shaped short story follows Mara through the closure of a lost-property office, using linked encounters to build a quiet, bittersweet narrative.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant, dryly funny, and tender without insisting that its characters’ small disappointments become grand revelations. Mara’s work gives the story a humane premise: people often arrive asking for a missing object and, as they talk, reveal what they are really trying to recover. The anecdotes about the ladder, the goat, the bean, and the keys accumulate into a sense of lives connected by ordinary acts of attention. The ending invites the reader to see Mara’s practical help with the girl’s zip as meaningful—not a cure for loss, but a way of taking care of what is immediately in front of her.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds lost and mislaid objects as carriers of memory, guilt, affection, and incomplete stories. It dwells on small, specific things—the ladder with a split rung, the brother’s index card, the bean in its jar, the sack of keys—and on the people who handle them. Its moral emphasis is modest: patience and generosity can help people find what they need, even when the original object is gone or the larger problem remains unresolved. The closing movement from the office’s keys to the girl’s envelope and stuck zip extends that concern into a simple act of care.

## Evidence line
> She was good at persuading people to tell her what was actually missing.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the story’s recurring lost-object motif, consistent understated humor, and repeated turn toward practical tenderness make its chosen emotional register especially clear.
